idiom_name: createContext<T | null>(null) plus a throwing useSelect() hook; generic parent flows the value type
implementation_notes:
The typed React realization: hold the family's contract in the context type - createContext | null>(null) with a useSelect() hook that throws on null - so every child reads the shared state with the value type inferred, and the parent's props can be a discriminated union that makes mutually exclusive configurations (single vs multiple selection) unrepresentable. A generic parent (Select) flows the option value type into the children, which the untyped form cannot express; export the context type alongside the components so consumers building their own children can subscribe. As in plain JavaScript, prefer context over cloning elements, because cloneElement's typing (ReactElement

with Partial

) can only add props the child's declared type already knows about.
pitfalls: createContext<T>(defaultValue) forces an invented default: use null (or undefined) plus a hook that throws, so misuse is a runtime error with a message rather than a wrong value.

The context is not generic per consumer - a Select<number> and a Select<string> share one compiled context type, so the parent must cast at the provider and the child's type alone cannot guarantee agreement.
Children from another package cannot be typed into the family; the runtime check remains necessary even when the types look complete.
Inlining the context value object re-renders every consumer; memoize it (or split state and dispatch) as in the untyped form.

variants.name: Angular content projection: ng-content plus ContentChildren/DI parent lookup
variants.implementation_notes: Angular's realization is content projection: the parent's template places <ng-content>, the call site's children are projected into it, and the parent finds them with @ContentChildren (or the signal-based contentChildren query) to wire behaviour - Angular's own documentation gives exactly this pattern for menus, tabs and lists, which use ContentChildren to find their children and wire up behaviour such as keyboard navigation, focus management and ARIA attributes. Children get the parent through DI, either by injecting the parent component (optionally restricted with @Host/@Optional) or by receiving whatever the parent provides, so no shared prop is threaded through the call site. Typing pays off twice here: the query is typed to the child directive/component, and the parent's provided state can be typed as an interface a child injects.
variants.idiom_name: ng-content projection with @ContentChildren queries and constructor injection of the parent component
pitfalls: Projected content is not automatically traversed: without ContentChildren (or contentChildren) the parent sees the call site's markup only as opaque DOM.
Content projected into a nested element escapes an <ng-content> selector unless the query recurses (descendants: true) - children silently miss the parent's state.
DI resolution walks the injector hierarchy, so a child placed outside the parent's element subtree gets a different (or no) provider - mark the injection @Optional and fail loudly.
ContentChildren queries are resolved after view init; code that reads them in the constructor sees an empty list.

variants.name: Typed custom element family: declaration-merged JSX intrinsics plus ElementInternals
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript's platform variant adds static checking to the native realization: the custom element is typed as an HTMLElement subclass with required attributes as properties, and a declaration merge into JSX.IntrinsicElements (the JSX namespace the TypeScript handbook describes) teaches the JSX type checker about the new tag, so a family can be used from TSX without a framework. Registration and form participation are the same as in JavaScript - slotchange plus assignedElements for the child set, static formAssociated + ElementInternals for form submission - and the types only cover the element's own surface: children are still discovered at runtime, so the parent must fail loudly when nothing usable is assigned.
variants.idiom_name: customElements.define + slot/assignedElements registration + typed JSX.IntrinsicElements augmentation
pitfalls: Declaration merging only types the element's own attributes: children and their required attributes remain unchecked, so runtime validation is still on the parent.
Typing the element as HTMLElement loses the attributes unless they are declared as properties or an attribute map is provided - consumers then cast everywhere.
The JSX augmentation is global: a wrong or duplicated declaration (from a dependency) silently overrides yours, so keep it in a small, importable .d.ts.
ElementInternals is only typed in recent TypeScript DOM libs; an older lib version compiles the class but rejects setFormValue.
